passage: In their small house behind the Kota bus depot, Himani had learned to read Vikas's footsteps. Some evenings he came home with jalebis and sat close, telling her she was his whole world. Other times he barely spoke for days, and she tiptoed round the kitchen, afraid any word would push him further away. Last month she caught herself rehearsing a simple "How was work?" three times before saying it. That frightened her more than his silences. So she went back to her Saturday embroidery class with her cousin. She told Vikas, "I love you. But I can't keep guessing which you will walk in. I'd like us to see a counsellor, and I'm keeping my Saturdays either way." He didn't answer that night. On Saturday she went anyway.

qa.q: What did Vikas sometimes bring home?
qa.a: He sometimes came home with jalebis.

qa.q: What frightened Himani most last month, and why?
qa.a: She caught herself rehearsing a simple question three times, and it frightened her because it showed how carefully she had been tiptoeing around him.

qa.q: What turning point did Himani choose?
qa.a: She went back to her embroidery class and told Vikas she loved him, wanted them to see a counsellor and would keep her Saturdays, looking after herself instead of trying to fix him.

qa.q: How might Vikas feel hearing Himani's calm limit?
qa.a: He may feel unsettled or defensive at first, which may be why he doesn't answer, but her steadiness gives him something consistent.

grounding: A young wife confused by her husband's warmth and sudden distance protects her own wellbeing, stays steady and suggests professional help.

passage: In their Berlin flat, Fatima found Olga's sticky note on the fridge: "Best weekend ever. Love you endlessly." Two days later Olga moved her things to the sofa and wouldn't meet her eyes. It had happened four times since spring. Fatima kept apologising for things she hadn't done and checking her phone for Olga's mood. One evening, on a video call with her sister, she heard herself say, "I've shrunk." That night she told Olga calmly, "I care about you. I can't fix this for you, and I'm going to stop trying. I think a therapist could help you, and I've booked one for myself too." Olga cried, then went quiet. In the morning Fatima went for her usual run.

qa.q: What did Olga's sticky note say?
qa.a: It said, "Best weekend ever. Love you endlessly."

qa.q: What does Fatima mean when she says "I've shrunk"?
qa.a: She feels she has lost herself, always apologising and checking Olga's mood out of confusion and fear.

qa.q: What choice did Fatima make that evening, and why was it wise?
qa.a: She calmly stopped trying to fix Olga, suggested a therapist for Olga and booked one for herself, protecting her own wellbeing.

qa.q: How might Olga feel when Fatima says she will stop trying to fix things?
qa.a: Olga may feel upset and scared, which may be why she cries and goes quiet, yet she also hears a steady, caring message.

grounding: A woman confused by her partner's sudden affection and distance stops walking on eggshells, protects herself and encourages professional support.

passage: Parul, you asked how I knew when to stop tiptoeing. When I was twenty-four I was engaged to Vinod. One week he'd send me poems and turn up at the bank with jasmine. The next he'd vanish, and when I called he'd say, "Why are you always after me?" I learned to watch his face before I spoke, to weigh every word. I stopped seeing my friends in case he needed me. My turning point was small: I fell ill with worry before an exam, and lying in that clinic I thought, I'm disappearing. I told him I loved him and that I'd keep my Sunday walks with my friends, no matter what. And I asked him, gently, to see a counsellor. We didn't marry, but I kept myself. That's Vandana-masi's one lesson.

qa.q: What did Vinod bring to the bank?
qa.a: Jasmine.

qa.q: What was young Vandana feeling while she watched Vinod's face before speaking?
qa.a: She felt anxious and confused, always on guard and afraid of setting off his coldness.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the story?
qa.a: Falling ill before an exam made her see she was disappearing, so she kept her friends and asked Vinod to see a counsellor.

qa.q: How might Vinod have felt when Vandana kept her Sunday walks?
qa.a: Vinod may have felt unsettled or hurt, but also met a steady limit instead of her tiptoeing.

grounding: Shows a young adult confused by a partner's hot-and-cold behaviour, who protects her wellbeing and encourages professional help.

passage: With his accountancy exam six days away, Pranav couldn't afford another week like the last one. On Monday Asif had cooked his favourite biryani and kissed his forehead. By Wednesday he'd stopped speaking, slammed cupboards and slept on the sofa. Pranav caught himself tiptoeing to the fridge, rehearsing sentences before saying them, forgetting whole pages of notes. On Thursday he packed his books and told Asif, calmly, "I love you. I'm going to study at my sister's till the exam. I'm not leaving you; I'm looking after myself." Then, softer: "The ups and downs scare both of us. Will you talk to a counsellor about it?" Asif's jaw tightened. Then he nodded, once.

qa.q: Where did Pranav go to study?
qa.a: To his sister's.

qa.q: How was Pranav feeling during the week before he packed his books?
qa.a: He felt confused and on edge, tiptoeing and rehearsing sentences, so anxious he forgot pages of notes.

qa.q: Why was going to his sister's a wise step?
qa.a: It protected his wellbeing and exam while he stayed warm and consistent and encouraged professional help.

qa.q: What might Asif be feeling when he nods?
qa.a: Asif may feel hurt and scared, yet accept that the swings are hurting both of them.

grounding: Illustrates a partner confused by sudden affection then distance, who protects his wellbeing and encourages counselling.

passage: Irfan checked Naina's mood the way other people checked the weather. On Friday she'd hugged him at the door of their Hyderabad flat and planned a trip to Coorg; on Sunday she wouldn't look at him and called him clingy for asking why. At lunch on Monday, his friend Sahil noticed him rewording a message for the tenth time. "You're walking on eggshells, bhai." Irfan admitted he'd stopped going to cricket in case she needed him. Sahil said, "You can't fix her by shrinking. Keep your cricket. Be steady. And ask her, kindly, to talk to someone who can help." That evening Irfan went to cricket, came home at nine as promised, and told Naina he loved her and hoped she'd see a counsellor.

qa.q: What had Irfan stopped doing?
qa.a: Going to cricket.

qa.q: What was Irfan feeling as he reworded the message for the tenth time?
qa.a: He was anxious and confused, afraid of setting off Naina's coldness.

qa.q: What did Sahil advise, and why is it wise?
qa.a: Keep cricket, be steady and kindly suggest help, because Irfan cannot fix Naina by shrinking himself.

qa.q: How might Naina feel when Irfan comes home at nine as promised?
qa.a: Naina may feel reassured by his consistency, even if the suggestion of a counsellor is hard to hear.

grounding: Shows a partner walking on eggshells in a hot-and-cold bond who protects his own life, stays consistent and encourages professional help.

passage:
"Last night you brought me flowers and said I was the best thing in your life," Manoj said. "This morning you won't look at me."
Omkar stirred his coffee. "I just need space."
"That's what you said last week, after the trip. And the week before."
"So now I'm the problem."
"No. But I've started checking your face before I speak. I'm walking on eggshells in my own home, Omkar, and I don't like who I'm becoming."
Omkar went quiet.
"I love you. I'm still going to be here, same as always. And I'm going to keep my evening runs and my Friday dinners with friends, whatever mood you're in."
"...Okay."
"And I think you should talk to someone about this. A therapist. Not because you're broken. Because this hurts you too."

qa.q: What did Omkar bring Manoj last night?
qa.a: He brought him flowers.

qa.q: How is Manoj feeling about the hot-and-cold pattern?
qa.a: Manoj feels confused and on edge, checking Omkar's face before speaking and not liking who he is becoming.

qa.q: What wise steps does Manoj take instead of trying to fix Omkar?
qa.a: He stays consistent, protects his own wellbeing by keeping his runs and Friday dinners, and encourages Omkar to see a therapist.

qa.q: How might Omkar feel when Manoj says "This hurts you too"?
qa.a: Omkar might feel less blamed and more understood, since Manoj frames it as care rather than calling him broken.

grounding: Shows a partner confused by sudden affection then distance, who protects his wellbeing, stays consistent and encourages professional support.
